confirmed_problem: F02 and F03 metadata wrappers previously called requirements with default new mode. Their explicit table-service override could therefore replace legacy configuration even though YqlSelect was disabled.
checked_contracts: Native metadata dispatch supplies mode only to wrappers declaring that argument; existing two-argument metadata and requirements-only generators retain their interfaces.
Both affected wrappers forward the requested mode while preserving the default new mode for existing direct callers.
The exact post-override settings and YqlSelect dictionary are checked before subprocess execution; unknown, duplicate or contradictory flags fail closed.
Both stale legacy wrappers are rejected before the mocked process is called, and anonymous descriptors are closed by the existing finally path.
Requested and effective fallback flags are separately recorded; explicitly enabled fallback controls remain ordinary semantic tests.
Exclusive C37/C38 comparisons require complete mode evidence, matching settings digest and fallback disabled on both sides.
An actual C44 fallback-enabled generator passes through run_generated, retains fallback, and still checks base-table and index-table contents; it cannot satisfy exclusive-comparison proof.
Future explicit contradictory mode evidence fails record_verdict. Historical records without these new fields retain their prior narrower verdict except where exclusive proof is newly required.
The helper records requested optimizer configuration rather than claiming proof of the engine route actually executed.
limitations: No actual native process or compiler was run. The prospective patch has not been applied to active helpers by this reviewer.
Historical records without settings identity cannot be upgraded to mode-proven evidence by this review.
Fallback-enabled success establishes functional behavior through the permitted route, not execution exclusively under new RBO.
Configured optimizer identity is distinct from runtime trace proof; existing semantic and provenance contracts remain necessary.
